title: Rethlas, Archon and Danus: Agentic Frameworks for Mathematical Research
body: # Mathematics Research Agents Recently, large language models have improved dramatically and now perform strongly on various mathematical benchmarks and IMO problems. However, real mathematics research is very different from problem solving in math competitions. It involves proposing interesting and meaningful conjectures to explain observed phenomena; investigating toy examples or hunting counterexamples to accumulate intuitive understanding; developing theories that provide tools for possible proofs; understanding the literature on previous research; and finally solving problems by applying established theories and verified results, without the limited syllabus or restricted scope of a math olympiad. ## Rethlas and Archon Earlier this year in April, an AI-for-Math team led by Professor Bin Dong at Peking University developed [Rethlas](https://github.com/frenzymath/Rethlas) [1], an open-sourced autonomous agent system for solving problems in mathematical research. It consists of a generation agent and a verification agent, and solves the stated problem autonomously via a generate–verify loop until a pre-set maximum number of iterations is reached or a verifier-approved solution is produced. The generation agent mimics the workflow of a mathematician, encoded as agent skills (toy examples, counterexamples, decomposition, etc.); it chooses which skill to apply based on the state of its investigation, and intermediate artifacts such as constructed examples, abandoned plans, and verification reports accumulate in a persistent working memory rather than disappearing when the model's context window fills. The verification agent reads a candidate proof the way a referee would: it checks each step, expands definitions from their source context, and confirms that every cited result exists and says what the proof needs it to say; if it finds critical errors or gaps, the proof goes back to the generation agent with repair hints. The generation agent is augmented by a theorem retrieval tool called **Matlas** [5], developed by the team earlier. The Matlas system, available at [https://matlas.ai/](https://matlas.ai), is a theorem search engine built from 8.51 million statements collected from 435K published papers across 180 journals and over 1,900 textbooks; a query is a mathematical statement, and retrieval is by meaning rather than keywords. It provides a more reliable and curated source of mathematical results, and in addition it extracts statement dependencies and performs hierarchical unfolding to make statements more self-contained. This provides the agent with the capability of reliable literature search comparable to that of human experts. Rethlas has solved a number of research problems autonomously, partially listed at [Rethlas_results](https://github.com/frenzymath/Rethlas_results). For example, it solved a technical algebraic group theory problem on rational conjugacy classes of 1-parameter subgroups in 44 minutes, using base model GPT-5.5 xhigh. This problem was brought to us by Professor Brian Conrad at Stanford University, who also helped verify the output of Rethlas. By contrast, GPT-5.5 Pro, given the same problem through its web interface, produced a confidently written but completely incorrect proof. This difference demonstrates the power of the harness: performance depends not only on the base model but also on how information, tools, state, and feedback are exposed to it. In [1], Rethlas is paired with an autonomous formalization agent, called [Archon](https://github.com/frenzymath/Archon), to ensure machine-checkable correctness. Archon translates informal arguments into fully formalized Lean 4 projects through structured task decomposition, iterative refinement, and automated proof synthesis, equipped with our formal theorem search engine LeanSearch; internally it splits its work between a planning agent and a proving agent. Therefore, Rethlas and Archon together form an end-to-end automated framework for tackling research-level mathematical problems with minimal human intervention. Using this framework, we automatically resolved an open problem in commutative algebra proposed by D. D. Anderson (2014) and formally verified the resulting proof in Lean 4. Rethlas found a new counterexample in about 45 minutes; the key ingredient, a 2006 result of Jensen from the distant generic-formal-fiber literature, was surfaced by Matlas, a connection that would ordinarily require collaboration between experts from different fields. Archon then formalized the entire construction — 19,448 lines of Lean 4 across 42 files, completed in about 80 hours of agent runtime — autonomously filling nontrivial gaps that were omitted or left implicit in the informal proof and its references. *The end-to-end pipeline: Rethlas's generate–verify loop (left) produces an informal proof; Archon (right) compiles it into a kernel-checked Lean 4 project.* ## Danus However, for more complicated and subtle research problems, a linear generate–verify loop oversimplifies the workflow of mathematicians: in real research, a mathematician needs to gradually accumulate many small facts and pieces of progress, and to adjust strategies and plans dynamically, before eventually resolving the problem. Sometimes it also requires the collaboration of several mathematicians, exploring different approaches with different domain expertise. The team recently developed and open-sourced [**Danus**](https://github.com/frenzymath/Danus) as a more powerful reasoning system that scales mathematical reasoning agents to long-horizon research problems [2]. Danus is an orchestration system centered on a shared fact graph, a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that serves as the global memory-management mechanism. It consists of a main agent that performs planning and coordination; several generation agents (workers) that carry out proof search in parallel and collaborate over the shared fact graph; and a stateless verifier that checks proposed mathematical claims before they are admitted into the fact graph. The main agent periodically summarizes the evolving proof state, redirects workers across promising directions, and supports interaction with human mathematicians through progress reports. The design follows a strict separation of powers, enforced with tools rather than instructions: no agent may both steer the search and decide what is true. The main agent (Claude Opus 4.8 on Claude Code) performs no mathematical derivations and has no tool for submitting facts, so the agent that steers the search cannot introduce unverified claims into the record; it may consult GPT-5.5-pro at a limited rate for strategic advice. The workers (generation agents as in Rethlas) each take a single claim at a time — a lemma, a counterexample, a toy computation — and revise it under verifier feedback until it passes. The verifier is instantiated fresh for each submission and is the sole authority on correctness. Under careful harness engineering, the verifier produces essentially no false positives, and this reliability is load-bearing: with 499 facts chained into one theorem, even a 1% per-fact error rate would drive the probability that the whole chain is sound below 1%. *Danus's role separation: the main agent plans but cannot submit facts; workers propose one claim at a time; a stateless verifier is the sole gate into the fact graph.* Each node of the fact graph is a verifier-accepted fact (statement plus checked proof), and each edge is a logical dependency; the fact graph is the system's unique source of truth. Everything else — plans, hunches, dead ends, GPT-5.5-pro's advice — lives in a separate memory that is explicitly not truth. If a fact is later found wrong, revocation removes it together with all transitive dependents. The fact graph is what lets the system grow in both width and depth: the proof decomposes into units that individual workers can own, so parallel contributions accumulate instead of colliding, and information is condensed as it moves upward (worker logs into a shared global memory, global memory into the main agent's summaries), so what any single agent must read stays bounded while what the system knows keeps growing. Once the target theorem appears as a verified fact, a writing subsystem turns the fact graph into a paper-style manuscript, which is then re-verified as a whole; citations are captured as data at proof time and the bibliography is assembled from those records, which prevents hallucinated references structurally. As a test, Danus was run on a then-open problem posed by Stanford math PhD candidate Ronnie Cheng on tangent classes for matroid building sets: construct, for every loopless matroid and building set, a class in the integral K-ring that specializes to the tangent bundle in the realizable case, recovers the graded dimensions of the Chow ring through Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch, and satisfies Chern-number lower bounds matching projective space. This reproduces the main theorems of Cheng's paper [4], which was deliberately withheld from every system and was not yet on arXiv when the experiment ran. The same verbatim prompt went to three systems: | System | Setup | Outcome | |---|---|---| | GPT-5.5 Pro (web) | the web product: search + long thinking | no solution | | Rethlas | three independent runs, same worker/verifier models as Danus | nothing passed the verifier | | Danus | 7 workers, ~5 days, 13 GPT-5.5-pro consultations | complete verified solution | The final fact graph held 3,157 verified facts connected by 8,616 dependency edges, with dependency chains up to 54 deep; the global memory recorded 636 proof attempts, 151 counterexamples, and 25 dead ends. There was only one human mathematical intervention: Danus declared the task finished after constructing the rational class, and the authors pointed out that the original problem asked for the integral one, after which Danus resumed and built the integral lift. The result is now a paper by Cheng and me [3], with an appendix by Gao and me, whose body is a faithful presentation of Danus's output. *The final fact graph of the matroid run: 3,157 verified facts produced by seven workers over about five days.* ## Human–AI collaboration These agentic systems suggest that human–AI collaboration can be very beneficial in mathematical research when it is done right. AI can help humans hunt for possible counterexamples to conjectures, prove technical lemmas in a paper, or even prove main theorems in certain cases. Although the examples above are (almost) autonomous, a human in the loop is still needed. At the very least, a human expert is needed to propose a clearly stated and meaningful question. And although formalization tools such as Archon in Lean 4 can serve as reliable proof checkers, Mathlib is still under development and its scope falls behind current mathematical research in many subjects, so in most cases a human expert is still needed to verify AI outputs carefully. Moreover, AI reasoning is grounded in the existing literature and lacks the capability of theory building: AI still needs humans to set up abstract theories and novel machinery, and sometimes needs human hints when it gets stuck. Even for Danus, when no foothold exists the system circles the problem, accumulating shallow local conclusions without breaking it open, until a human names the missing ingredient. **Humans supply direction; the machine supplies verified execution and its own repairs.** Humans posed the problems, occasionally supplied references, and at stall points told the system what was missing. In the work on the first open case of the foliated Shokurov index conjecture, Danus split the problem into five classes on its own and solved three via a Lie-theoretic route the experts on the project had not anticipated; those three were the hard ones, in the same experts' judgment. It stalled on the two cases humans find easy until a single hint, "foliated minimal model program," unblocked them. When an error was found, the repair was always carried out by the system, not the human. The interaction, as the Rethlas paper puts it, resembles explaining a proof to a graduate student: indicate key difficulties, point out errors, supply references, without spelling out the details. **The collaboration goes beyond proving well-posed statements.** In a $p$-adic Hodge theory collaboration, human mathematicians proposed an initial conjecture and Rethlas proved it, exposed a redundant hypothesis, sharpened a "for genus large enough" assumption into an explicit bound, and, asked whether that assumption could be dropped, constructed a counterexample imported from a topic so distant that the human authors said they might never have found it themselves. Therefore, the system helped the mathematicians understand the problem and refine its correct formulation. ## Conclusion | System | Main contribution | |---|---| | **Rethlas** | Autonomous informal reasoning: mimics the workflow of human mathematicians by combining reasoning primitives with our mathematical theorem search engine Matlas inside a generate–verify loop | | **Archon** | Autonomous formalization: informal proofs compiled into kernel-checked Lean 4 projects, navigating Mathlib via **LeanSearch**, with a plan/prove dual-agent design | | **Danus** | Orchestration of several parallel workers over the **fact graph**, a shared verifier-gated memory DAG of established facts, coordinated by a main agent which plans and interacts with humans | ## References [1] H.
